profile.background: An adult who shares a house with two friends and volunteers to wash the team bibs for a recreational walking group. They enjoy the weekly outing.
profile.history: They recall an earlier episode of very muddled thinking and later discussions about schizophrenia at the outpatient clinic. Lately keeping track of several small tasks has felt difficult.
profile.organization: Has a general sense of the sequence of events but related thoughts can pull attention away from the point. Concrete details are easier to recall than broad summaries.
profile.spontaneity: Likes to talk and often notices extra details while remembering an event.
profile.guardedness: Open about the walking group but dislikes the impression that they cannot manage responsibilities.
profile.expression: Good-humored about minor mistakes and disappointed when an unfinished job affects someone else.
profile.self_understanding: Notices that having several things needing attention at once makes it easier to lose track.

facts.content: Before last week's walk they put the clean team bibs by the door and got distracted looking for a bus card. A friend reminded them to take the bag.
facts.disclosure_context: A little embarrassed, particularly about other people waiting.

facts.content: It is easier to lay out things for the group in the evening, when the kitchen is quiet.
facts.disclosure_context: An observation they can discuss comfortably.

facts.content: They put their bus card in the pocket of the bib bag after the last walk.
facts.disclosure_context: Pleased to have found a practical arrangement.

facts.content: A housemate sometimes reads the day's jobs back to them while they gather things.
facts.disclosure_context: Comfortable receiving help from this person.

facts.content: They keep their medication in its labeled pack and remember the next outpatient appointment because it falls the day after the group walk.
facts.disclosure_context: These are familiar details of their week.

dialogue.question: What have you been looking forward to lately?
dialogue.answer: “The walking group—I always look forward to our weekly outing. I wash the team bibs, so I’ve got those to get ready as well. It’s easier to lay everything out in the evening when the kitchen’s quiet. Oh, and I put my bus card in the bib bag after the last walk, so that’s one less thing to hunt for. Quite pleased with that little arrangement!”

dialogue.question: What would you like to talk over while you're here?
dialogue.answer: “I’d like to talk about keeping track of things when there are several little jobs at once. Last week I had the clean bibs by the door, then went looking for my bus card, and a friend had to remind me to take the bag. All washed and ready, and nearly left behind! I felt a bit embarrassed—I don’t like keeping people waiting. Putting the card in the bag should help with that bit, but it’s the losing track I’d like to talk over.”

dialogue.question: When does everything get a bit much?
dialogue.answer: “When there are several little things needing attention at once. Like last week—the bibs were ready, but then I was looking for the bus card and nearly went without the bag. The washing was done; it was getting everything out the door together! I don’t like the thought of everyone waiting on me. It’s easier to lay things out in the evening when the kitchen’s quiet. Sometimes my housemate reads the jobs back to me while I gather things, and that helps me keep track.”

dialogue.question: I mean keeping track of several jobs. Are there particular times when that feels easier or harder?
dialogue.answer: “In the evening, when the kitchen’s quiet, it’s easier to lay things out for the walk. It’s harder when several little jobs need attention together—I can get one done and lose track of the next. The bibs were washed, you see; it was remembering the bag while looking for the bus card that caught me out. Having my housemate read the jobs back while I gather things helps. And I’m quite pleased with keeping the card in the bag now—those two can travel together!”

dialogue.question: How do you usually get things together for the walking group?
dialogue.answer: “I wash the bibs, then lay things out in the evening when the kitchen’s quiet. Sometimes my housemate reads the jobs back to me while I gather everything—that helps if there are several bits to do. And now the bus card’s in the pocket of the bib bag, so I won’t be hunting for that separately. Clean bibs are all very well, but they do need to come along with me!”

dialogue.question: Could you give me an example of something you needed to remember before a recent outing?
dialogue.answer: “The bag of clean bibs for last week’s walk. I’d put it by the door, all ready, but then I went looking for my bus card and a friend had to remind me to take the bag. Done the washing and nearly left the whole lot behind! I was a bit embarrassed—I don’t like keeping people waiting. The card lives in the bag’s pocket now, so that’s one less thing to look for.”

dialogue.question: Does the order make a difference to you?
dialogue.answer: “Do you mean the order I do the little jobs in—washing the bibs, getting the bag ready, that sort of thing?”

dialogue.question: I mean the order in which you do your jobs. What difference does having a usual sequence make, if any?
dialogue.answer: “It helps to have one thing to do next, rather than several things needing attention at once. I can get one job done and then lose track of the next bit. The bibs were clean and by the door last week, but looking for the bus card took me away from remembering the bag. So the order helps, but there’s still getting everything out the door! I’m pleased the card’s in the bag now—one less separate thing to keep track of.”

dialogue.question: Who do you feel comfortable asking for help with a practical job?
dialogue.answer: “My housemate—the one who sometimes reads the jobs back to me while I gather things. I’m comfortable asking them. I can do the jobs; it’s keeping track when there are several little bits at once that gets tricky. Having someone read them back helps me stay with what I’m doing.”

dialogue.question: What do you do when two things need your attention at the same time?
dialogue.answer: “I can get pulled onto one and lose track of the other. That’s what happened with the bus card—the bibs were ready, but looking for the card took my attention off taking the bag. If my housemate reads the jobs back while I gather things, that helps. I can do the jobs; it’s keeping both in mind that’s tricky. At least the card and the bibs travel together now!”

dialogue.question: How do you remember when it's time for a clinic appointment?
dialogue.answer: “My next appointment is the day after the group walk—that’s how I remember it. The walk gives me something to go by: walking group first, clinic the next day.”

dialogue.question: Is there anything about your day-to-day life you'd like us to talk more about?
dialogue.answer: “Yes, how to keep track when there are several little jobs at once. I enjoy doing the bibs for the walking group, and I want to keep doing my bit. Having my housemate read the jobs back helps, but I’d like to talk about what I can do myself as well. It’s not the washing—it’s getting the finished job out of the door!”
